summary: Registers algorithms used by WebAuthn and FIDO2 CTAP in the IANA COSE Algorithms registry, including RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with several SHA hashes and certain elliptic curve signature algorithms.

eli5.summary: Login keys speak a particular language of codes, and this adds missing code names to the official list.

questions: which cose algorithms does webauthn use
why is rs1 deprecated in cose
subtitle: Registers the RSA and secp256k1 signature algorithms that WebAuthn and FIDO2 need in the COSE and JOSE registries.

tldr.problem: WebAuthn and FIDO2 CTAP implementations use COSE algorithm identifiers that were missing from the IANA registries, including RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 variants and ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to use these algorithms with COSE and JOSE, and registers RS256, RS384, RS512, RS1, ES256K and the secp256k1 curve with IANA.
tldr.outcome: All the new entries are marked as not recommended or deprecated, and RS1 MUST NOT be used by new COSE applications and protocols.

today: RFC 8812 is a Proposed Standard from August 2020, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. The algorithms it registers remain marked Not Recommended or Deprecated in its own registrations.

sections.title: Why These Registrations Exist
sections.content:
The W3C Web Authentication (WebAuthn) specification and the FIDO Alliance FIDO2 Client to Authenticator Protocol (CTAP) specification both use COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption, RFC 8152) algorithm identifiers. Some of the algorithms they use had no entry in the IANA registries.

This document registers five algorithms in the IANA "COSE Algorithms" registry and the secp256k1 curve in the "COSE Elliptic Curves" registry. For JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption, RFC 7515) it registers the matching ES256K algorithm and the secp256k1 curve in the JOSE registries.
sections.eli5: An official list of code names for signing methods was missing a few names that login systems already use. This document adds them.

sections.title: RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 Algorithms
sections.content:
The RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature algorithm is defined in RFC 8017 and is parameterized by a hash function. A key of 2048 bits or larger MUST be used, and implementations need to check that the key type is RSA when creating or verifying a signature.

Four COSE identifiers are registered: RS256 (-257, SHA-256), RS384 (-258, SHA-384), RS512 (-259, SHA-512) and RS1 (-65535, SHA-1). The first three are marked Recommended: No, and RS1 is marked Deprecated. These algorithms were already in the JOSE registry, so the registrations here are only for COSE.
sections.eli5: These are four versions of the same signing recipe, each using a different scrambling tool. None is the top pick, and the oldest one is flagged as outdated.

sections.title: secp256k1 and ECDSA Signatures
sections.content:
The SECG elliptic curve secp256k1 is written in a JSON Web Key as kty EC and crv secp256k1. In a COSE_Key it is kty (1) EC2 (2) and crv (-1) secp256k1 (8). In JOSE the uncompressed point encoding MUST be used, with x and y each exactly 256 bits. COSE allows either uncompressed or compressed points, with x exactly 256 bits.

The new algorithm identifier ES256K (-47) means ECDSA with secp256k1 and SHA-256. A signature is made by producing the pair (R, S), turning each into a 32-octet big-endian sequence without dropping leading zero octets, and concatenating R then S. The result is a 64-octet signature value.

Implementations SHOULD generate the ECDSA nonce deterministically, for example with RFC 6979. Because deterministic ECDSA has been shown to be susceptible to fault injection attacks on devices open to physical attack, implementations SHOULD add countermeasures where that is possible.

When used for ECDSA, secp256k1 MUST be used only with ES256K, not with ES256, which in JOSE is defined only for the P-256 curve. The RFC leaves use with ECDH-ES key agreement to experts in future specifications.
sections.eli5: secp256k1 is a particular shape of mathematical curve used to make signatures. The document says exactly how to write down the key and the signature, and that it must only be paired with its own special label.

sections.title: What IANA Registered
sections.content:
IANA registered the following, all with the IESG as change controller:

  • COSE Algorithms: RS256, RS384, RS512, RS1 and ES256K, as described above.
  • COSE Elliptic Curves: secp256k1, value 8, key type EC2, Recommended: No.
  • JOSE Algorithms: ES256K, usage location alg, implementation requirement Optional.
  • JSON Web Key Elliptic Curves: secp256k1, implementation requirement Optional.
sections.eli5: The keepers of the official list wrote each new name and number into the right lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSA key size guidance from Section 6.1 of RFC 8230 applies. The security notes for RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-2 from Section 8.3 of RFC 7518, including the exponent restrictions, also apply, which is why those algorithms are registered as Not Recommended.

RS1 is Deprecated because of the concerns about SHA-1 in RFC 6194. It is registered anyway because deployed Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) still use it, so WebAuthn implementations need an identifier to represent TPM attestations. New COSE applications and protocols MUST NOT use it.

For secp256k1, a key could be mistaken for a P-256 key, since their representations differ only in the crv value. The only defense currently available is restricting the set of curves used. Scalar multiplication that does not run in constant time permits timing side-channel attacks. The RFC also notes theoretical weaknesses of the curve that could lead to future attacks, which is why it is registered as Recommended: No.
sections.eli5: Most of these methods come with a caution label. The oldest one stays on the list only because some hardware still uses it, and nobody new should pick it.
